implementation_notes: Since C++17 a function, or a type returned by value, can be marked [[nodiscard]], so dropping the result of a call is a diagnosable mistake unless the caller writes an explicit (void) cast; the standard library models the rule itself - emplace_back returned void until C++17 and returns a reference since, and operator<< returns the stream so insertions chain. Return the computed value, use std::optional when absence is normal and std::expected (C++23) when absence needs a reason, and keep void for operations that genuinely have nothing to report. The classic out-parameter form is still justified when a call must produce several outputs or an existing signature must be preserved, but returning a small value or struct is clearer and allows copy elision.
pitfalls: [[nodiscard]] is a warning, not an error: (void) discards it, and some compilers only report it under -Wall/-Wextra, so the team has to decide how far to escalate it.
Marking a whole type [[nodiscard]] applies to every function returning it by value, which forces a cast at every deliberate discard.
Returning *this from a mutator breaks value semantics: a fluent chain mutates one object, cannot be used on a const or temporary receiver, and can prevent copy elision.

variants.name: Fluent self-returning methods (pre-C++17 style)
variants.idiom_name: *this chaining: fluent setters/builders and stream insertion
variants.implementation_notes: The receiver-returning realization: every setter or builder step ends with return *this; so construction reads as a single expression - C++ made this idiomatic for I/O by having operator<< return basic_ostream&, and ostringstream chains follow the same shape. Choose it when the caller's expected next act is another call on the same object, and keep it away from queries, because returning *this erases the command/query distinction and hides that the object was mutated. This is also the form for toolchains older than C++17, where [[nodiscard]] does not exist, or when an existing fluent API has to be preserved.
pitfalls: A *this chain requires the object to outlive the whole expression: a temporary or const receiver cannot be chained, and chaining on a shared object mutates state for every user of it.
Every step returns the same object, so the chain cannot produce a new value - callers who wanted a copy must ask for one explicitly.

variants.name: std::expected result chaining (C++23)
variants.idiom_name: std::expected<T, E> with transform / and_then / or_else
variants.implementation_notes: Return std::expected so the value and the reason it may be missing travel together, then chain with transform/and_then/or_else so the caller keeps acting on the result instead of unwrapping it into a status variable. Mark the producing helpers [[nodiscard]] as well, because expected itself does not warn when it is dropped. Prefer it over std::optional when the absence has a cause worth propagating, and over exceptions when failure is a normal, expected domain outcome.
pitfalls: std::expected is C++23: older toolchains need tl::expected or Outcome, whose types do not interoperate with the standard one.
Mixing exceptions and expected results in one API forces every caller to handle failure twice.
